title: Can AI Help Activate "Explorer Mode"?
author: Jeff Lippman
summary: Jeff Lippman, a school head, draws on Anderson and Winthrop's The Disengaged Teen to ask when AI in schools supports student agency instead of draining it. He sets a seventh grader's 'magic pen' metaphor, in which AI makes work easier while making students less creative, against the story of a twelfth grader who built a study app after noticing he was avoiding the friction that learning requires. The app tracks where the student loses marks and generates targeted practice, and building it gave him authentic experience with metacognition, quality evaluation, user feedback and data protection. Lippman argues this is a move from consumer to producer rather than cognitive offloading. He proposes two dials for judging any classroom use of AI, agency and intellectual friction, and asks whether each goes up or down.
points: The 'Achiever Mode' versus 'Explorer Mode' framing gives schools a vocabulary for judging whether AI use keeps students compliant or builds real agency.
A student's 'magic pen' metaphor captures the genuine risk that AI makes work faster while making it less the student's own.
The most instructive AI use in the story was a student building a tool that sent him back toward the material he was avoiding, not away from it.
Building with AI can develop evaluation, metacognition, resilience and awareness of data protection in ways that using AI to finish assignments does not.
Before approving a classroom use of AI, ask whether agency will rise or fall and whether intellectual friction will be preserved or smoothed away.
quotes: Most schools are organized to to keep students in “Achiever Mode” where they are working hard and getting excellent results. In those schools, students make very few decisions about their own learning and their success comes mainly through complying to adult expectations.
Of course the problem is that as AI seeps into the learning environment, it often drains the very agency we are trying to promote.
AI is like a magic pen; it can write your work faster and with more detail than you had imagined. But the more you use it, the less creative you become and the less the work is your own.
he realized that he was actively avoiding the friction necessary for learning.
For João, using AI to build his app and refining it so that it matches its purpose was not a shortcut. There was no “cognitive offloading” here.
Instead it enabled him to go from being a consumer to a producer. It gave him real authentic experience with quality assessment and evaluation.
I think the answer lies in thinking about two dials that measure agency and intellectual friction. As we think about using AI with our students we should monitor the dials.
